project.name: SINTEF Impact Story
project.description: Groups improve the content of SINTEF's 5-slide Impact Story: the problem, SINTEF's contribution, the impact pathway, downstream potential and the public-facing story. Each group works on one SINTEF result: use the case the facilitator gives you, or agree on one in the first minutes and name it in your first contribution. Lofn turns your group's input into slide-ready text for every field.
project.synthesisGuidance: Write the answer as draft content for the slide. Use the slide's field names as bold lead-ins, in the order they appear on the slide (for example **A real-world problem:** …). Start with one line naming the case or SINTEF result the group is working on. Keep each field short enough to fit on the slide: one or two sentences, about 35 words at most. Use only facts, figures, partners, quotes and sources the group contributed; never invent them. Keep evidence labels (OBSERVED, ESTIMATE, SCENARIO) whenever contributors give them, and keep activities and outputs distinct from outcomes and impacts. When a field has no supported content yet, write [still missing: …] and say what evidence or decision is needed. Put sources, caveats and longer detail in a final section headed 'Speaker notes'. Use open questions for weak links and unsupported claims, and disagreements for competing wordings or interpretations.

questions.title: Slide 1: Why does this problem matter?
questions.instructions:
Improve each field of the slide:
• A real-world problem: name the affected user or setting. What is hard, risky or costly today? Describe it without project jargon.
• Who is affected: the people, organisations or systems that bear the burden.
• Scale: one or two sourced indicators, with unit, place and year. No good number? Use a documented case or quote.
• If nothing changes: the continuing harm or lost opportunity, and who bears it.

Evidence: give the source and date of every figure, and say whether it is an established baseline or a modelled estimate.
Quality check: could someone outside the project explain the problem after 15 seconds?

Good contributions: draft wording for a field, a concrete example, a number with its unit, year and source, or a challenge to a weak claim. Text, voice notes and photos (e.g. of a sketch) all work.

questions.title: Slide 2: What did SINTEF contribute?
questions.instructions:
Improve each field of the slide:
• Before: the limitation that existed before this work. Name strong existing alternatives fairly.
• SINTEF result: the method, technology, dataset, standard or insight, in plain language, with its maturity (e.g. validated algorithm, demonstrator, evidence base for policy).
• New capability: what a named user or partner can now do.
• Distinct role and partners: what SINTEF added, and what partners contributed.

Evidence: the report, publication, prototype, benchmark or partner confirmation behind it, with dates or versions for performance claims.
Quality check: if SINTEF's contribution disappeared, what would be materially different?

Good contributions: draft wording for a field, a concrete example, a number with its unit, year and source, or a challenge to a weak claim. Text, voice notes and photos (e.g. of a sketch) all work.

questions.title: Slide 3: How does the result create impact?
questions.instructions:
Improve each field of the slide:
• Mechanism: the chain from research result → integration or transfer → adoption → changed practice → direct outcome → lasting benefit. Name who is accountable at each step.
• Adoption: who uses it, how often and at what scope.
• Outcome: the measured change against a baseline or comparison, with unit and scope.
• Benefit: the documented effect for users.
• Source, counterfactual and attribution: study or partner record, sample, date, comparison, and SINTEF's share of the credit.

Evidence ladder: activity (a workshop happened) → output (a guideline was published) → outcome (users changed a process) → impact (a meaningful benefit followed). Don't relabel outputs as impacts. A patent or publication is not proof of adoption.
Quality check: where is the weakest link, and what would have happened anyway?

Good contributions: draft wording for a field, a concrete example, a number with its unit, year and source, or a challenge to a weak claim. Text, voice notes and photos (e.g. of a sketch) all work.

questions.title: Slide 4: What are the downstream effects and the potential?
questions.instructions:
Improve each field of the slide:
• Observed direct effect: one outcome evidenced on slide 3, with unit and date.
• Downstream effects: economic, environmental, societal and knowledge consequences that follow from it. Name the mechanism, who is affected, the direction of change and the time horizon. Include rebound effects or costs.
• Scale (scenario): eligible users × adoption share × net benefit, with stated assumptions. Keep the labels OBSERVED, ESTIMATE and SCENARIO.
• What unlocks it: the barrier, the action, its owner and a target date.
• Dependencies, trade-offs and assumptions: what must hold, who might bear a cost, and which decision is needed next.

Quality check: can someone reproduce the total from the assumptions? Is the same benefit counted twice?

Good contributions: draft wording for a field, a concrete example, a number with its unit, year and source, or a challenge to a weak claim. Text, voice notes and photos (e.g. of a sketch) all work.

questions.title: Slide 5: What is the impact story? (the public-facing slide)
questions.instructions:
This slide must make sense on its own. Use only claims that survived the discussion of slides 1 to 4.
• Headline: a human headline about the change in a person's life, an organisation's work or a real system. Not the project acronym.
• SINTEF contribution: one sentence on what SINTEF developed or established, and with whom.
• Photo or 15–30 second video: who or what it should show (consented, real, captioned).
• Why it matters: the immediate outcome, the benefit to people or systems, and the wider possibility.
• Three numbers at most: an observed result, adoption or reach, and (clearly marked) a potential scenario. Each with unit, timeframe and status.
• Quote: an approved, attributed quote from a person or partner, or a documented plain-language finding instead.

Publication check: who or what changed? What did SINTEF contribute? What proves it? Why does it matter? What could happen next?

Good contributions: draft wording for a field, a concrete example, a number with its unit, year and source, or a challenge to a weak claim. Text, voice notes and photos (e.g. of a sketch) all work.

cycles.name: Round 1: Draft the slides
cycles.note: Agree on your case, then fill as many fields as you can across the five slides. Rough is fine; numbers and sources help most.

cycles.name: Round 2: Strengthen the evidence
cycles.note: Lofn starts from your Round 1 answers. Challenge weak claims, add sources and numbers, cut jargon, and fill the fields marked [still missing].
